section.title: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin
section.sectionRationale: The healing of the lame man and Peter's sermon in the temple provoke the first official clash between the church and the Sanhedrin, the very council that had condemned Jesus. Peter and John are arrested, examined, and forbidden to speak in the name of Jesus, yet the word keeps spreading and the number of believers grows to five thousand. Threatened and released, the apostles return to the church, which prays not for safety but for boldness, and the passage closes with a picture of a community so gripped by the resurrection that no one counts his possessions his own.
section.thesis: The risen and exalted Christ is Himself the rejected stone now made the cornerstone, the one name under heaven by which anyone is saved, and when His witnesses are threatened for that name the church answers with prayer for boldness, receives a fresh filling of the Spirit, and lives out a resurrection generosity that leaves no one in need.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the arrest at the temple as the resurrection is preached; the examination before the council where Peter names Jesus as the only saving name; the council's helpless threat and the apostles' refusal to be silent; the church's prayer for boldness and its answer; and the shared life of a people transformed by grace.

units.label: Arrest at the temple
units.note: seized for preaching the resurrection, yet the number grows to five thousand

verses.text: While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them,
greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead.
They seized Peter and John, and because it was evening, they put them in custody until the next day.
But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand.

units.label: By what name? The only name that saves
units.note: the rejected stone is the cornerstone; salvation in no one else

verses.text: The next day the rulers, elders, and scribes assembled in Jerusalem,
along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and many others from the high priest’s family.
They had Peter and John brought in and began to question them: “By what power or what name did you do this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers and elders of the people!
If we are being examined today about a kind service to a man who was lame, to determine how he was healed,

then let this be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed.
This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the {{akrogoniaios|cornerstone}}.’
{{soteria|Salvation}} exists in no one else, for there is no other {{onoma|name}} under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”

units.label: The name forbidden, yet we cannot stop speaking
units.note: the council marvels at their boldness but forbids the name

verses.text: When they saw the {{parresia|boldness}} of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they marveled and took note that these men had been with Jesus.
And seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response.
So they ordered them to leave the Sanhedrin and then conferred together.
“What shall we do with these men?” they asked. “It is clear to everyone living in Jerusalem that a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it.
But to keep this message from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.”
Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John replied, “Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God.
For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
After further threats they let them go. They could not find a way to punish them, because all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.
For the man who was miraculously healed was over forty years old.

units.label: The believers' prayer for boldness
units.note: the church prays not for safety but for courage, and the place is shaken

verses.text: On their release, Peter and John returned to their own people and reported everything that the chief priests and elders had said to them.
When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord. “Sovereign Lord,” they said, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
You spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David: ‘Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?
The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His {{christos|Anointed One}}.’
In fact, this is the very city where Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed.
They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.
And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness,
as You stretch out Your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.”
After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.

units.label: One in heart and soul
units.note: resurrection generosity leaves no one in need; Barnabas the encourager

verses.text: The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned.
With great power the apostles continued to give their testimony about the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. And abundant grace was upon them all.
There were no needy ones among them, because those who owned lands or houses would sell their property, bring the proceeds from the sales,
and lay them at the apostles’ feet for distribution to anyone as he had need.
Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (meaning Son of Encouragement),
sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

onoma.gloss: Name; and in Hebrew and Greek thought far more than a label, it stands for the person himself, his authority and presence. The lame man was healed in the name of Jesus, and Peter presses the point to its edge: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Salvation is not a technique or a philosophy but a Person, and to invoke His name is to lean the whole weight of one's rescue on Him.

soteria.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue, and the wholeness that follows. The same root that healed the lame man's body reaches to the healing of the whole person before God. Peter declares that this rescue exists in no one else; the God who raised Jesus offers full deliverance in Him alone, and refusing that name is to refuse the only lifeline given to humanity.

akrogoniaios.gloss: The corner, the cornerstone or head of the corner. Quoting Psalm 118:22, Peter tells the builders of Israel that the very stone they rejected in crucifying Jesus is the one God has set as the cornerstone of His new temple, the people He is building. What the authorities discarded God has made the load-bearing stone on which everything now rests.

parresia.gloss: Boldness, frank and fearless speech, the freedom to say openly what must be said. The council marvels that unschooled men speak with such freedom, and later the church prays for still more of it. This boldness is not natural temperament but the fruit of the Spirit and of having been with Jesus; it is the courage to keep naming His name whatever the cost.

christos.gloss: Anointed One, the Christ, the Messiah; the Greek rendering of the Hebrew Mashiach. Praying Psalm 2, the church sees the raging of the nations against the Lord and His Anointed fulfilled in the plot against Jesus, God's holy servant whom He anointed. The rulers meant to destroy the Messiah; instead they carried out exactly what God's hand had planned, and the Anointed reigns.

basic.context: Peter has just healed a man lame from birth and preached Jesus in the temple. Now the temple authorities, especially the Sadducees who denied any resurrection, arrest Peter and John for teaching that Jesus rose from the dead. The next day the same Sanhedrin that condemned Jesus questions them. Peter, filled with the Spirit, tells them plainly that the man was healed by the name of Jesus, the stone they rejected, and that there is no other name that saves. Threatened and warned to stop, the apostles say they cannot be silent, and the church responds by praying for boldness.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the first collision between the risen Christ's witnesses and the religious power that killed Him. The heart of it is Peter's speech, and its peak is verse 12: salvation in no other name. Notice how the story keeps contrasting human threat with divine power: the council can imprison and forbid, but it cannot deny the miracle or stop the word. The believers' prayer in verses 24 to 30 shows us how the early church read its own suffering through Scripture, especially Psalm 2.
basic.originalLanguages: Several words carry the passage. The onoma, the name of Jesus, means His very person and authority, and it is the one name that saves, offering soteria, full rescue. Peter quotes Psalm 118 to call Jesus the rejected stone made the akrogoniaios, the cornerstone. The council marvels at the apostles' parresia, their bold and fearless speech, and the church prays Psalm 2 about the plot against God's christos, His Anointed One.
basic.typology: The rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone is a picture Jesus applied to Himself; Israel's builders reject Him, and God makes Him the foundation of a new temple, His people. The persecuted witnesses who cannot stop speaking foreshadow the whole line of faithful confessors. The shared possessions of the church echo the promise that in God's people there would be no poor among them.
basic.christ: Christ is the whole point. He is the name by which the man was healed, the crucified one whom God raised, the rejected stone now the cornerstone, and the only name under heaven that saves. The prayer names Him as God's holy servant and Anointed One, against whom the rulers raged in vain, fulfilling exactly what God had planned. The apostles preach a living Lord, not a dead teacher.
basic.god: God is the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth, who spoke by the Spirit through David, and whose hand and will had already decided what the rulers would do. He raises the dead, He heals, and He fills His people with courage. He is not threatened by the Sanhedrin; He answers threats by shaking the room and filling His witnesses afresh with the Spirit.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 118:22 supplies the rejected stone. Psalm 2:1-2 is the prayer's text about the nations raging against the Anointed. 1 Peter 2:4-8 develops Christ as the living cornerstone. Deuteronomy 15:4 promised there would be no poor among God's people, echoed in the church's generosity.
basic.oneStory: The ascended Christ has poured out His Spirit, and now the gospel meets its first resistance from the very authorities who crucified Him. But the rejected stone is now the cornerstone, and the one name that saves cannot be silenced. From Jerusalem the word keeps spreading, and a new community forms, marked by boldness in witness and grace in sharing, the first outworking of the mission that will reach the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Luke gives the chapter its backbone with one word, 'name.' The council asks 'By what power or what name,' verse 7. Peter answers 'by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth,' verse 10, and says there is 'no other name under heaven,' verse 12. The council decides to warn the apostles 'not to speak to anyone in this name,' verse 17, and commands them 'not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus,' verse 18. The church ends its prayer asking God to heal 'through the name of Your holy servant Jesus,' verse 30. The one issue in dispute is whose name carries authority.

A second thread is boldness. The Greek noun parrhesia, 'freedom of speech,' is what the council sees in the apostles in verse 13, what the church asks for in verse 29 and what the church receives in verse 31, when 'they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.' Prayer for boldness is answered by boldness, and the structure shows it.

The movement is in four scenes with a private room in the middle. The arrest, verses 1 to 4, leads into the public interrogation, verses 5 to 12. The council then sends the apostles out and confers in private, verses 15 to 17, where Luke lets the reader overhear what the apostles cannot, that the rulers admit the miracle is undeniable and still resolve to suppress it. The threat follows, verses 18 to 22, and then the church's prayer, verses 23 to 31. The chapter closes with a summary of shared life, verses 32 to 35, and a single named example, Barnabas, verses 36 and 37, which prepares for the contrasting example in chapter 5. Even the interrogation is a reversal of roles. The apostles are made to stand 'in the midst' as the accused, but by the end of the scene it is the council who have 'nothing to say in response,' verse 14.
context.historical:
The captain of the temple guard was the priest in charge of order in the temple precincts, and the Sadducees were the aristocratic party that controlled the priesthood. They denied the resurrection of the dead, so a teaching that 'in Jesus' the resurrection had happened struck at the root of their theology as well as their authority. The Sanhedrin that met the next day was the high court of the nation, and its leading figures are named: Annas, who had been high priest and whose family held the office in turn, Caiaphas, who presided at the trial of Jesus, and others of the high priest's family. Luke names them so that the reader knows these are the same men who had condemned Jesus only weeks before.

To be 'unschooled, ordinary men,' verse 13, did not mean illiterate. The Greek describes men without formal training in the schools of the scribes, and laymen without office. Peter and John were Galilean fishermen, and their lack of credentials was striking in a court of professional teachers. What the council could see was that these men had been 'with Jesus,' a phrase that reaches back to the way Jesus had called disciples 'to accompany Him,' Mark 3:14.

The verdict of the council also reveals the politics. They cannot deny a miracle done in front of the whole city, and they fear the people. Luke says the rulers 'could not find a way to punish them, because all the people were glorifying God,' verse 21. The man's age matters here: he was 'over forty years old,' so he had been lame his whole adult life, and half of Jerusalem had walked past him.

The shared life of the believers took place in a city with large numbers of the poor, including many pilgrims and widows. A sale of land to fund distribution was a costly act in an economy where land was the main store of security, and the care of the poor was a recognised duty in Israel, Deuteronomy 15:7 to 11. Barnabas is a Levite from Cyprus, a Jew of the Dispersion, and his appearance here anticipates the part he will play when he vouches for Saul, Acts 9:27, and when he brings the gospel to Antioch, Acts 11:22 to 26.
context.canonical:
The 'rejected stone' is one of the most persistent images in the Bible. Psalm 118:22 and 23 sang of a stone that the builders threw out and God made the cornerstone, 'marvelous in our eyes.' Isaiah spoke of a tested cornerstone laid by God in Zion, on which a believer will not be shaken, Isaiah 28:16, and of a stone of stumbling for those who will not trust, Isaiah 8:14. Jesus applied the psalm to Himself in the parable of the tenants, Matthew 21:42 and Luke 20:17 and 18, adding that whoever falls on the stone will be broken. Peter, who now quotes it to the council, comes back to it in 1 Peter 2:4 to 8, where the stone is both precious to those who believe and an offence to those who do not.

The prayer of the church uses Psalm 2, which was probably the coronation psalm of David's line. The nations rage against the LORD and His Anointed, and the LORD answers from heaven. The early church saw Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel's leaders in the psalm's raging kings, and so read the cross as the moment when the psalm's conspiracy was enacted and defeated. Paul quotes Psalm 2:7 of the resurrection, Acts 13:33, and the risen Christ promises its iron sceptre to those who overcome, Revelation 2:26 and 27.

The exclusivity of verse 12 belongs with Jesus' own saying, 'No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6, and with Paul's, 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,' 1 Timothy 2:5. The shared life of verses 32 to 37 takes up the old promise of Deuteronomy 15:4, 'There will be no poor among you,' and the later churches take up the pattern in another form, in the collection for the saints in 2 Corinthians 8 and 9, which Paul grounds in Christ who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see how the church behaves when it is first threatened by the authorities. It does not retreat or retaliate. It tells the truth about Jesus, refuses to stop, goes to its own people, and prays. The prayer is the heart of the chapter: it reads the opposition by Psalm 2 as part of God's plan, and it asks for boldness rather than rescue.

He also means to argue that the apostles' message cannot be made private. When the council commands silence, Peter and John do not claim a right to speech. They say they must obey God, and that they cannot stop reporting what they have seen and heard, verses 19 and 20. The authority of their witness lies in what they saw and in the One who sent them. Luke's account makes it plain that the council's real difficulty is not any lack of evidence. They have a healed man standing before them.

Finally, Luke places the lived generosity of the church beside its bold testimony as two proofs of the same grace. The 'abundant grace' that is upon them, verse 33, shows in a community where no one is needy, verse 34. Barnabas is held up as a pattern of that grace: he is named 'Son of Encouragement,' and he gives his field quietly. Luke wants readers to be both bold in their testimony and open-handed with their goods, because the same risen Christ is the source of each.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records three kinds of event. The arrest and trial are descriptive of what happened to two named men; the church is not told to expect arrest or to seek it. The prayer of verses 24 to 30 is both description and a model. Its shape, naming God as Creator and Sovereign, reading the threat by Scripture, asking for boldness and expecting God to act, is one that believers have followed ever since. The shaking of the building and the fresh filling are God's response, and the text does not make them a formula for how every prayer will end.

The shared life of verses 32 to 37 is the hardest case. The summaries are written in a pattern that sounds as if everyone sold everything, yet Luke gives a single named example, Barnabas, and in the next scene Peter will tell Ananias that the land was his to keep, Acts 5:4. The sharing was real, voluntary and responsive to need, and it was not a law. What it teaches is that grace makes people hold their possessions loosely and look for the poor among them.

The clearest prescriptive material is the exclusivity of the name and the principle of obeying God over human command, verses 12, 19 and 20, which Peter repeats in Acts 5:29. Those are statements of what is true and of what is owed to God. They are not instructions for how to treat any particular government. For that, Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2 must be read with them.

debates.question: Does the sharing of possessions in verses 32 to 37 prescribe a form of community that all churches must adopt?

views.label: A description of Spirit-wrought generosity, not a binding structure
views.case: Luke presents the sharing as voluntary and Spirit-prompted; Peter later tells Ananias the land and its proceeds remained his own to give or keep, Acts 5:4, which shows ownership was not abolished. The abiding principle is love that meets need, expressed in ways fitting each setting, not a mandated common purse.

views.label: A pattern the church should seek to embody more fully
views.case: The repeated summaries hold this shared life up as beautiful and normative in spirit; the promise that there would be no poor among God's people is fulfilled here, and later churches are urged to give sacrificially so that there is equality, 2 Corinthians 8. So the passage does press every generation toward real, costly sharing.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the resurrection produces open-handed love that leaves no brother or sister in need; they differ on whether the specific first-Jerusalem form is a required structure or a Spirit-shaped principle to be applied wisely in every context.

debates.question: Does 'no other name' mean that people must hear and confess the name of Jesus to be saved?

views.label: Salvation requires knowing and trusting Jesus by name
views.case: Peter says there is no other name given among men by which we must be saved, verse 12, and Paul says that people cannot call on One in whom they have not believed or believe in One of whom they have not heard, Romans 10:13 to 15. On this view the verse is the ground of missions: the nations are lost without the gospel, and that is why Christ's witnesses must go.

views.label: Christ alone saves, but God may bring some to Him without full knowledge
views.case: Others hold that the verse names the only ground of salvation, the person and work of Jesus, without settling how widely God gives the knowledge that saves. They point to the faith of Old Testament believers who looked ahead to a Saviour they did not know by name, and to Peter's own words that God welcomes from every nation those who fear Him, Acts 10:34 and 35. They stress that this is not a claim that other religions save.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that salvation is found in Jesus alone and in no religion, teacher or achievement beside Him. They differ about the reach of the knowledge needed. The verse itself is not a statement about the unreached but a bold claim made to a hostile court, and its natural effect is to send the church out to tell everyone.

debates.question: How does 'We must obey God rather than men' relate to the call to submit to rulers?

views.label: Obedience to rulers is real but limited by obedience to God
views.case: Paul says that everyone must submit to governing authorities, since they are appointed by God, Romans 13:1, and Peter tells believers to submit to every human institution, 1 Peter 2:13. Yet the same apostles refuse a direct command to stop proclaiming Christ. The midwives did the same in Exodus 1:17, and Daniel's friends in Daniel 3:16 to 18. Authority is given by God, so it cannot rightly command what God forbids.

views.label: The refusal is narrow and non-violent
views.case: Others stress how little the apostles claim. They do not resist arrest, they do not call for the overthrow of the rulers, and they accept flogging and imprisonment. They disobey only where the command would silence the witness to Christ, and they pray for boldness, not for revenge. On this view the passage gives a very limited license for civil disobedience and an unlimited duty of witness.

debates.bearing: All agree that the limit comes where a ruler commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands. The debate is how often that happens and what form the refusal should take. The apostles' example is public, truthful, willing to suffer and free of violence.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's choice of the word 'name,' onoma, matters because in the ancient world a name stood for the person and his authority. To act 'in the name' of someone meant acting with his backing, and to ask 'by what name' was to ask who stood behind this man. Peter's answer, 'the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth,' puts the crucified man from Galilee in that place.

In verses 9 and 12 Peter uses the same Greek verb for two things English separates. In verse 9 the man 'has been healed,' sesotai, from sozo. In verse 12 the name is the one 'by which we must be saved,' sothenai, from the same verb. Luke's readers would have heard the connection at once: the rescue of the man's legs is a picture of a deeper rescue. The word 'must,' dei, also returns from Acts 3:21, the same word that marked a divine necessity. Salvation is not one possible route among others; it is something God has laid down. Peter also says the name was 'given,' dedomenon, so the name is a gift from God and no human invention.

Verse 11 quotes Psalm 118:22 with two changes. Peter says the stone was 'rejected' by 'you builders,' and the verb he chooses, exoutheneo, means to treat as nothing and to hold in contempt. He also adds 'you,' pointing the line at the council. The 'cornerstone' is literally the 'head of the corner,' kephale gonias, which can mean the foundation stone at the angle or the capstone that completes the building. Either way the stone is chief.

In verse 13 the council sees 'boldness,' parrhesia, a word built from 'all' and 'speech.' It is the freedom to say everything, and it is a frequent word in Acts for fearless witness, as in verses 29 and 31. The apostles are called 'unschooled, ordinary men,' agrammatoi kai idiotai, literally 'without letters' and 'private persons.' The English word 'idiot' descends from the second term, but its ancient sense was simply someone with no public office or special training. The reason for their boldness is given in a phrase echoing the Gospels: 'they had been with Jesus.' A servant girl had used the same expression of Peter in the courtyard, Luke 22:56, and now it is a verdict in his favour.

In verse 19 Peter says, 'Judge for yourselves,' krinate, which turns the judges into the judged. He says 'we cannot stop speaking,' using a form that means 'we are not able not to speak.' The word 'listen' in verse 19 is akouo, which was the verb at the heart of Moses' command about the prophet to come, 'You must listen to Him,' Acts 3:22.

The prayer opens with 'Sovereign Lord,' despotes, a term for a master who owns slaves, and in verse 29 the church calls itself His 'servants,' douloi, slaves. In verse 27 and verse 30 Jesus is God's 'holy servant,' pais, the same word that is used of David in verse 25. The verb for 'anointed,' echrisen, in verse 27 is the verb behind the title christos. And God's 'hand and will,' verse 28, had 'decided beforehand,' proorizo, the same family as the 'set plan' of Acts 2:23. The request that He 'stretch out' His hand, verse 30, uses the language of the exodus, as in Exodus 6:6.

Verse 32 describes the believers as 'one in heart and soul,' and says they held things 'in common,' koina, as in Acts 2:44. It is the language of Greek friendship, which held that friends share all things, and also of Israel's call to love God with all the heart and soul. The name 'Barnabas,' verse 36, is explained as 'Son of Encouragement,' huios parakleseos, from the same root as the word for comfort or exhortation.

typology.type: The stone the builders rejected, Psalm 118:22
typology.fulfillment: In its first setting the psalm celebrates a king or a people despised by the nations and then lifted up by the LORD. In Jesus the pattern is exact and greater: the rulers of Israel, the builders, reject Him and God raises Him as the cornerstone of a new temple. Jesus quoted the verse of Himself, Luke 20:17, and Peter says it before the very men who did the rejecting. The escalation is that the building is not a nation's fortunes but God's own house of living stones, 1 Peter 2:4 and 5. The type falls short in that the psalm does not mention a death, and the resurrection is the proof the psalm could only hint at.

typology.type: The raging kings and the Anointed, Psalm 2:1-2
typology.fulfillment: The psalm described the nations plotting against the LORD and His Anointed, a King of David's line. The church prays that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel did exactly this in the one city. The escalation is that the conspiracy of the nations, which the psalm saw as hopeless, actually took place and actually served God's purposes: they did what His hand and will had decided beforehand, verse 28. The psalm goes on to say that the LORD laughs and sets His King on Zion, and the resurrection is that vindication, Acts 13:33. The type is incomplete, since the final rule 'with an iron scepter' still lies ahead, Revelation 2:27.

typology.type: The year of the Lord's favor and the end of poverty, Deuteronomy 15:4
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law looked for a day when 'There will be no poor among you,' and the year of release and jubilee gave that hope a calendar. Jesus opened His ministry by proclaiming 'the year of the Lord's favor,' Luke 4:19. In the early church the hope is acted out in a community where 'no needy ones' remained, verse 34. The correspondence is real, but the church's sharing is only a first fruit, since the poor will not cease from the land in this age, as Jesus says in John 12:8. The final fulfilment is the new creation, where there is no more pain or want.

typology.type: The disciple before the same court as the Master
typology.fulfillment: The council asks Peter and John a question it had put to Jesus, 'by what authority,' Luke 20:2, and the answer comes from men who had once run away. Jesus told His followers that a servant is not greater than his master, and that if they persecuted Him they would persecute them, John 15:20, and He promised that the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say, Luke 12:11 and 12. The pattern is that the witnesses share the Master's trial, His boldness and His vindication. The pattern falls short in that the apostles are not saviours, and they point away from themselves to the name.

study.christ:
Christ is at the centre of the chapter in three ways: as the name, as the stone and as the Anointed One. The council asked about power and name, and Peter's whole reply is Jesus. The man stands healed 'by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead,' verse 10. Peter builds the statement on two pairs, man and God, crucified and raised, which hold the whole gospel.

The stone is the image Jesus chose for Himself. In the parable of the tenants He quoted Psalm 118 and added that anyone who falls on the stone will be broken, and that the one on whom it falls will be crushed, Luke 20:17 and 18. Peter now stands before the builders and tells them to their faces that the stone is the very man they cast away. The reversal is a statement of the resurrection. The Jesus whom the highest court condemned has been set by God at the corner of everything that will stand. Isaiah's cornerstone, 'a sure foundation,' Isaiah 28:16, and the stone of stumbling, Isaiah 8:14, belong together: the same Christ is the foundation for those who believe and a cause of falling for those who do not.

Then there is the exclusive claim. 'Salvation exists in no one else,' verse 12. This is not Peter's idea but Christ's, 'No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. What Jesus has that no other has is both the person and the work: He is the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy 2:5, who has given Himself for all. The claim is made in a court, and its force is not arrogance but the logic of a rescue. If one rope reaches a drowning man, to say so is kindness.

The prayer carries a further Christology. Jesus is God's 'holy servant,' the one whom God 'anointed,' verse 27. David called himself God's servant in the psalm, and the greater Servant has now been anointed in the full sense, with the Spirit at the Jordan, Luke 3:22 and 4:18, and by His resurrection. In Psalm 2 the Anointed One is also the Son, and the church sees the Father's Son in the One against whom Herod and Pilate set themselves. The final line of the chapter shows the generous side of the same Lord. Barnabas lays a field at the apostles' feet, and the apostles testify with 'great power' to 'the resurrection of the Lord Jesus,' verse 33. Everything the community does is an answer to the resurrection.

The risk in a chapter this rich is forcing every detail into a picture of Jesus. The healed man, the field and the money are not coded portraits. The links rest on what the chapter itself says: the name, the stone and the Anointed One. The chapter's generosity is also an echo of the Lord's own self-giving, who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and that is the reason that Paul later gave for the church's giving.
study.god:
The church's prayer is the best window into the doctrine of God in this chapter. It begins with 'Sovereign Lord,' and then names Him as the Creator of 'the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,' verse 24. This is the first move Hezekiah made when Sennacherib's threatening letter arrived. He spread it out before the LORD and said, 'You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth,' Isaiah 37:16. The believers begin where he began, with the size of God, because a threat looks different in the light of the Creator. The rulers are creatures in a world He made.

God is the author of Scripture. The prayer says that He 'spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David,' verse 25. The words of the psalm are David's and God's, and they are also living: written long ago and exactly suited to this day. God is therefore a God who speaks beforehand and whose word proves reliable.

He is sovereign over the very people who oppose Him. Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen,' verse 28. This does not make God the author of their sin or lessen their guilt, since the church calls them conspirators. It means no plot against Christ can step outside the boundary God has set. The church is comforted not because the danger is small but because the God who planned the cross is the God who hears them now.

He is the God who answers. The place is shaken, a sign of His presence, as the doorposts shook at the voice of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:4 and as the nations will be shaken in Haggai 2:7. The people are filled again with the Holy Spirit. The request for boldness is met immediately. Repeated fillings in Acts show that being filled with the Spirit is not a single event but a continuing supply, as Paul's command to 'be filled with the Spirit' in Ephesians 5:18 also suggests.

He is the God who gives priority to the word. The church does not ask for the threats to be removed. It asks that it may go on speaking with complete boldness. And He is a God of grace in the community. 'Abundant grace was upon them all,' verse 33, and it appears as a household where no one lacks.

For worship, the prayer teaches us to address God by His greatness and to read our troubles by His word. It also teaches us what to ask. The believers do not ask for safety but for courage, and for His hand to continue to heal in the name of Jesus. The right response to threat is to gather, to pray with one voice and to leave the outcome with the One who decided the end of the story before it began.

crossReferences.note: The stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone, and the psalm calls it the LORD's doing and marvelous in our eyes. Jesus applies it to His own rejection, Matthew 21:42, and Peter applies it to the council, adding that the builders are the very ones standing before him.

Peter returns to the stone, joining Psalm 118, Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14. The stone is precious to those who believe and a stone of stumbling to those who do not. It shows what the apostle learned in the Sanhedrin: the same Christ is the foundation for some and the cause of falling for others.

Jesus promised that when His followers were brought before rulers and authorities, the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say. Peter, 'filled with the Holy Spirit,' verse 8, gives a courtroom defence that is not defensive at all but a plain preaching of Christ.

The nations rage, kings take their stand and rulers gather against the LORD and His Anointed One. The church's prayer reads this text as a description of what happened to Jesus in Jerusalem and what is now being done to His witnesses, and takes comfort from the fact that the psalm's God holds the throne.

The chief priests, scribes and elders ask Jesus by what authority He acts in the temple. The question is put again to His apostles in Acts 4:7. Jesus answered with a counter-question that exposed their evasion, while Peter answers directly. The scene shows the council's attitude has not changed.

Hezekiah spread a threatening letter before the LORD and prayed, naming Him as the God who made heaven and earth and asking Him to see and hear. The prayer of Acts 4 follows the same pattern of beginning with God's greatness before asking Him to consider the threat.

The law's promise that there will be no poor among God's people if they obey. Acts 4:34 records that there was no needy person among the believers, and Luke's wording sounds like a fulfilment. The church gives what Israel was told to give, because the Lord has poured out His grace on it.

A servant girl said of Peter in the courtyard, 'This man also was with Him,' and he denied it. In Acts 4:13 the council recognises the same fact about him and John, and he does not deny it. The phrase that once condemned his courage is now the explanation for it.

Peter says the same thing again before the same council: 'We must obey God rather than men.' The repetition shows that the answer given in 4:19 and 20 is not a passing remark but a settled principle that governs how the church deals with authority.

Paul says there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. It states in the language of the letters the exclusive claim Peter makes in Acts 4:12, and it shows that the early church was united in confessing that salvation has one source.

Paul grounds the church's giving in the grace of Christ, who was rich and became poor so that others might become rich. This is the root of the generosity described in Acts 4:32 to 37, and it shows that the sharing of goods is a response to the gospel and not a social programme.

Jesus opens His ministry with good news to the poor and the year of the Lord's favor. The believers' care so that none among them is needy is the continuation of that ministry in His body, and it shows that the Spirit who anointed Jesus is now at work in His people.

Paul says that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, then asks how they can call without hearing, and how they can hear without someone to preach. It is the reason the apostles cannot stop speaking, and it shows why an exclusive name carries an urgent mission.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that the Bible raises from its first pages: how can anyone be saved from a ruin that humanity cannot repair? Genesis 3 ended with a promise that a descendant of the woman would crush the serpent, and the story since has been the search for that deliverer. Acts 4 gives the answer in a single name. The one who was rejected, killed and raised is the only rescuer, and every earlier shadow of salvation, the ark, the exodus, the temple, the sacrifices, finds its meaning in Him.

The rejected stone ties together a story of rejected deliverers. Joseph was thrown into a pit by his brothers and became the saviour of his family, Genesis 37 to 50. Moses was refused by his own people, 'Who made you ruler and judge?', and became their redeemer, Acts 7:35. David was despised by his brothers and then anointed king. Each of these was a shadow of the stone that Israel's builders would throw away and God would set at the corner.

The chapter also advances the story of the Spirit. At Pentecost the Spirit was poured out on a waiting church; here He is given again in answer to prayer in the face of threats, showing that the gift is not a single event but a living supply for every new test. The church moves from the upper room to the temple court to the council chamber and back to a house of prayer, and at each stage the Spirit goes with it.

The sharing of goods is also part of the larger story. In Eden God gave a whole garden and the people lacked nothing. After the fall, scarcity and inequality entered the world, and the law tried to restrain them with sabbatical years and gifts for the poor. In the church the gift of the Spirit begins to undo the effects of the fall in the realm of possessions. It is not yet the new creation, and the next chapter shows sin still present, but it is a visible sign of what the new creation will be.

The chapter looks ahead to the end of the story as well. The nations that rage in Psalm 2 are finally put down, and the Anointed One reigns, Revelation 11:15 and 19:15. The name that the council forbade is the name that every knee will bow to, Philippians 2:9 to 11. The believers who pray for boldness in a room that shakes are the first members of a company who will one day stand without fear before the throne, and the shaking that Haggai promised will give way to a kingdom that cannot be shaken, Hebrews 12:28.

quiz.q: Why did the priests and Sadducees have Peter and John arrested?

options.text: They were disturbed that the apostles taught the people and proclaimed the resurrection in Jesus.
options.note: Verse 2 gives exactly this reason; the Sadducees denied any resurrection.

options.text: The apostles had healed a lame man in the temple.
options.note: The healing sparked the crowd and the sermon, but the stated offense was proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus.

options.text: The apostles were disturbing the peace with a riot.
options.note: There was a crowd, but Luke names the resurrection preaching, not disorder, as the cause of arrest.

options.text: They had spoken against Rome and Caesar.
options.note: The charge was religious, about Jesus and the resurrection, not political rebellion against Rome.

quiz.q: What does Peter declare about salvation before the council?

options.text: There is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved, only Jesus.
options.note: Verse 12 is the peak of Peter's testimony: salvation in no one else.

options.text: Jesus is the rejected stone whom God has made the cornerstone.
options.note: True and closely tied, from verse 11, but the explicit claim about salvation is the exclusive name in verse 12.

options.text: Salvation comes to those who keep the law of Moses faithfully.
options.note: Peter grounds salvation in the name of Jesus, not in law-keeping; this misplaces the emphasis.

options.text: Every sincere path leads to God in the end.
options.note: This directly contradicts Peter, who says there is no other name by which we must be saved.

quiz.q: How did Peter and John respond when ordered never to speak in the name of Jesus?

options.text: They said they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard, obeying God rather than men.
options.note: Verses 19 to 20 capture their refusal to be silent.

options.text: They asked the council to judge whether it was right to obey men rather than God.
options.note: They did say this in verse 19, but the fuller answer is their resolve that they cannot stop speaking.

options.text: They agreed to stop for a season to avoid trouble.
options.note: They did not agree to stop; they declared they could not be silent.

options.text: They fled the city to escape the council.
options.note: They did not flee; they returned to the church and prayed for more boldness.

quiz.q: What did the believers pray for after Peter and John were released?

options.text: That God would consider the threats and enable them to speak His word with complete boldness.
options.note: Verses 29 to 30 show they prayed for boldness, not for safety.

options.text: That God would stretch out His hand to heal and do signs through Jesus' name.
options.note: This is part of the prayer, but its central request is for boldness to speak the word.

options.text: That God would remove all persecution and give them a quiet life.
options.note: They did not ask for the threats to be lifted; they asked for courage in the face of them.

options.text: That God would send fire to destroy the Sanhedrin.
options.note: There is no such request; they prayed for boldness and for God's healing power.

quiz.q: What marked the shared life of the believers in verses 32 to 37?

options.text: They were one in heart and soul, sharing everything so that no one among them was in need.
options.note: Verses 32 to 34 describe this unity and generosity, with grace upon them all.

options.text: They pooled their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet.
options.note: True, as with Barnabas, but this was the expression of a deeper unity of heart and abundant grace.

options.text: They abolished private ownership as a permanent law for all churches.
options.note: The giving was voluntary and Spirit-prompted; Acts 5:4 shows ownership was not abolished.

options.text: They kept their goods to themselves and cared little for the poor.
options.note: The opposite is true; there were no needy ones among them.

questions: Peter and John were arrested for proclaiming the resurrection. Where in your own life does bearing witness to the risen Jesus feel costly, and what would faithfulness look like there?
Peter says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. How does the exclusivity of Christ sit with you, and how might you hold it with both conviction and compassion?

The council marveled that ordinary, unschooled men spoke with such boldness, and took note that they had been with Jesus. What might change in your witness if being with Jesus were your deepest habit?
When threatened, the church prayed for boldness rather than for safety. What do your own prayers under pressure tend to ask for, and how might this prayer reshape them?
The believers were so gripped by the resurrection that no one counted his possessions his own. Where is God inviting you toward more open-handed generosity so that others' needs are met?
Barnabas earned the name Son of Encouragement. Who has been a Barnabas to you, and whom might God be calling you to encourage in a concrete way this week?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered cornerstone translates a phrase that is literally the head of the corner, quoting Psalm 118:22; it names the chief stone that anchors the structure, which the New Testament applies to Christ.

Unschooled, ordinary men translates terms meaning without formal rabbinic training and private, that is, laymen. It highlights that their boldness came not from education but from having been with Jesus.
The prayer quotes Psalm 2:1-2. Where the text reads Anointed One, the underlying word is Christos, and a footnote notes the alternate renderings His Christ or His Messiah.
The word servant, also used in verse 30, can be rendered child; it echoes the servant of the Lord language of Isaiah applied to Jesus.
